title: Handling Underperformance
description: Addressing senior leader underperformance with observable expectations, fair support, careful documentation, compassion, and timely decisions.

competency.name: Handling Underperformance
competency.definition: Distinguishes skill gaps, role mismatch, motivation problems, and harmful behavior, then acts fairly and decisively.
competency.whyItMatters: When senior leaders tolerate unclear expectations or avoid difficult people decisions, teams absorb hidden delivery, trust, and morale costs.

prompt.primary: Tell me about a time you had to address underperformance in a senior leader.
variants: Describe a time when you waited too long to make a people decision.
Tell me about a time a well-liked leader was not scaling with the role.
Tell me about a time a talented leader's behavior was damaging team trust.
interviewerIntent: Can the candidate be fair and direct?
Do they distinguish role mismatch from character judgment?
Can they act decisively without losing compassion?
Do they recognize when harmful behavior needs boundaries rather than extended coaching?

scenario.signatureExample: An engineering director addresses a well-liked manager who is not scaling, while a VP faces a high-output leader whose behavior is damaging team trust.
context: The manager has strong trust with engineers but weak planning and delegation.
Team delivery depends too much on personal heroics.
Peers are frustrated by missed commitments but reluctant to criticize the person.
In harder cases, a leader may deliver results while creating fear, blame, or avoidable attrition risk.
constraints: The leader deserves clear expectations and support.
The business cannot keep absorbing delivery misses, hidden coordination cost, or trust damage.
The decision will signal how the organization handles performance.
Harmful behavior may require faster boundaries than a teachable skill gap.

storyAnatomy.situation: An influential leader was underperforming because the scope had outgrown their current capability or because their behavior was damaging trust.
storyAnatomy.task: Address the performance gap clearly and fairly while protecting the team and business outcomes.
action: Clarified **role expectations**, specific gaps, and the evidence that would change the decision.
Separated skill gap, role mismatch, motivation, and harmful behavior instead of treating every case as a generic coaching problem.
Rejected both immediate removal without evidence and open-ended support that would keep the team absorbing the cost.
Created a time-bound improvement plan when the gap was teachable, or set immediate behavioral boundaries when trust was being damaged.
Documented progress, support provided, team impact, and decision thresholds.
Changed scope, moved the person into a better-fitting role, or exited the leader when evidence showed the current scope was no longer viable.
result: Cross-team commitment misses fell from four in one quarter to one in the next planning cycle, and decision lead time for the affected area dropped from nine days to two.
Skip-level confidence in local leadership recovered from 3.1 to 4.0, while escalation volume about unclear ownership dropped by half.
The individual was treated respectfully, with either a better-fitting role or a documented exit path.
One roadmap area slowed by six weeks during the transition, but the team stopped absorbing hidden coordination and morale costs.
The organization saw that **performance expectations** were real, humane, and not dependent on popularity or output alone.
storyAnatomy.reflection: The hard lesson was that compassion without clarity prolongs stress for everyone involved.
systemChange: Clear manager expectations with evidence categories for planning, delegation, feedback, and collaboration.
Earlier performance calibration with peer, skip-level, and delivery signals.
Role-fit review before expanding management scope.
Behavior escalation rule for high-output leaders who damage trust.
Transition plan template covering succession, communication, and team protection.

exampleStories.title: Beloved Manager Not Scaling
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time a well-liked leader was not scaling with the role.
exampleStories.situation: A manager in a 45-person product area was trusted and well-liked, but was not delegating, planning across teams, or developing leads as the organization scaled. Three cross-team commitments slipped in one quarter because important decisions still routed through them.
strongAnswerSketch: Describe observable gaps in delegation, planning quality, and lead development rather than labeling the person.
Reject an immediate exit because the gap is teachable, but also reject another vague quarter of encouragement.
Clarify expectations and create a 60-day **coaching plan** with decision latency, planning quality, lead ownership, and commitment misses as evidence.
Move the person into a smaller, better-fitting role when the same gaps remain after the evidence window, while naming the residual cost: one delayed roadmap milestone and a frustrated peer lead.
whyItWorks: Models measurable evidence instead of relying on reputation.
Protects the team from prolonged ambiguity while admitting the transition cost.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I gave them feedback several times, but eventually it was clear they were not a fit and we had to move on.
followUpAngles: What exact expectation did they miss?
How long did you give the **coaching plan**?
What cost did the role change create?

exampleStories.title: Senior IC In A Lead Role Mismatch
exampleStories.promptVariant: Describe a time when you waited too long to make a people decision.
exampleStories.situation: A senior IC was made a team lead because of technical depth, but avoided feedback conversations and became a decision bottleneck. Two project leads started escalating around them, and sprint planning lead time grew from two days to more than a week.
strongAnswerSketch: Acknowledge the leadership design mistake instead of blaming the person.
Clarify whether the issue is skill gap, motivation, or role mismatch, using missed feedback conversations, decision latency, and team ownership as evidence.
Offer coaching and an alternate senior IC path, then remove lead scope when the same bottleneck repeats.
Admit the residual cost: a delivery slip and a trust reset with two project leads who had been waiting for action.
Change **promotion criteria** so future lead assignments require evidence of feedback, delegation, and conflict handling before scope expands.
whyItWorks: Creates a fairer leadership selection mechanism.
exampleStories.weakVersion: The person was not leadership material, so I replaced them with someone more people-oriented.
followUpAngles: How did you preserve the person's dignity?
What did waiting too long cost the team?

exampleStories.title: Talented Director With Corrosive Behavior
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time a talented leader's behavior was damaging team trust.
exampleStories.situation: A director owned a revenue-critical platform migration and hit delivery milestones, but publicly blamed managers in incident reviews, dismissed peer input, and created two regretted attrition risks in one quarter.
strongAnswerSketch: Separate high output from acceptable leadership behavior, and name the specific expectations being violated.
Use evidence from skip-levels, peer commitments, incident reviews, attrition risk, and direct observation so the case is not framed as a style conflict.
Reject ignoring the behavior because the migration is important, and reject a long generic performance plan that would leave the team exposed.
Set immediate behavioral boundaries, remove the director from people-management and incident-review authority after a repeat breach, and appoint an interim lead for the migration.
Manage the residual cost: the migration slows by four weeks, but skip-level safety improves, incident reviews become usable again, and peer leaders re-engage.
whyItWorks: Tests underperformance as harmful behavior, not only capability or role mismatch.
Shows fairness through evidence and direct expectations while protecting the team quickly.
Makes the rejected alternatives and cost of decisiveness explicit.
Demonstrates VP-level judgment about succession, communication, and organizational signal.
exampleStories.weakVersion: They were brilliant but difficult, so I coached them on communication until it became clear the team could not work with them.
followUpAngles: What evidence showed harmful behavior rather than a personality mismatch?
What boundary did you set before changing scope?
How did you protect the roadmap and the team after the decision?

strongAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate shows clear expectations, evidence, coaching, documentation, and timely action.
moves: Describes observable performance gaps rather than labels.
Separates skill gap, role mismatch, motivation, and harmful behavior before choosing the intervention.
Gives the person a fair chance with explicit expectations when the gap is teachable.
Sets faster boundaries when behavior is damaging trust or safety.
Measures progress and impact with delivery, team health, and ownership evidence.
Names rejected alternatives and the residual cost of the chosen path.
Acts when the situation does not improve.
Reflects on timing and system improvements.

weakAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate either avoids the issue or jumps to a cold termination without evidence, coaching, documentation, or learning.
redFlags: Cannot name the expectation the person failed to meet.
Confuses being liked with being effective.
Confuses high output with acceptable leadership behavior.
Delegates the hard conversation to HR or another leader.
Treats every case as coaching even when the behavior is harming the team.
Lets the situation continue until team trust is damaged.
Presents a clean win without naming the cost, rejected alternative, or transition risk.

followUps.question: What expectations did you make explicit?

strong: I named the role outcomes and behaviors: planning quality, delegation to leads, feedback cadence, decision ownership, and respectful disagreement in reviews.
For the director behavior case, I made the non-negotiables explicit: no public blame, no retaliation for escalation, and no bypassing peer decision rights.
weak: I told them they needed to communicate better and step up as a leader.
I explained that people were frustrated and that they needed to rebuild trust.

followUps.question: What support or boundary did you provide before making a final decision?

strong: For the scaling gap, I gave a 60-day plan, weekly coaching, a delegation checklist, and examples of planning artifacts that would meet the bar.
For the harmful behavior case, support included direct feedback and HR partnership, but the boundary was immediate: one repeat breach would remove people-management scope.
weak: I gave them feedback in our one-on-ones and told HR I was worried.
I tried to be supportive because I did not want the person to feel attacked.

followUps.question: Did you act too early, too late, or at the right time?

strong: I waited too long on the lead-role mismatch; two project leads had already started escalating around the person, so I changed the promotion trial design afterward.
I acted faster on the corrosive director because the repeated behavior was creating attrition risk and teaching the organization that results excused harm.
weak: I think the timing was right because I wanted to be fair and give them enough chances.
In hindsight maybe I waited too long, but these decisions are always difficult.

followUps.question: How did you manage the impact on the team?

strong: I named an interim owner, reset decision rights, told the team what would change without sharing private performance details, and tracked commitment misses, skip-level confidence, and escalation volume.
I acknowledged the roadmap slip openly, protected the team from more hidden coordination cost, and watched whether incident reviews and planning meetings became usable again.
weak: I reassured the team that we were handling it and asked them to stay focused.
I did not say much because performance matters are confidential.

signals.name: Clarity
signals.strong: Names expected outcomes, leadership behaviors, evidence, support, and **decision criteria**.
signals.weak: Relies on vague performance concerns or style judgments.

signals.name: Fairness
signals.strong: Uses consistent evidence, direct feedback, documented support, and clear boundaries before making a decision.
signals.weak: Surprises the person, skips feedback, or lets reputation dominate the evidence.

signals.name: Decisiveness
signals.strong: Acts at the right pace for the failure mode: coaching when teachable, faster boundaries when behavior damages trust.
signals.weak: Confuses compassion with delay or treats harmful behavior as merely a communication gap.

rubric.expected: Handles lead or manager performance in a focused area with concrete feedback, support, documentation, and team protection.
Distinguishes capability gaps from role mismatch across managers, uses calibration evidence, and changes scope before teams absorb repeated misses.
Makes senior leadership changes with fairness, speed, succession coverage, and a clear signal about what leadership behavior is tolerated.
Sets the company-level bar for executive behavior by separating recoverable gaps from trust-breaking conduct, aligning HR and succession coverage, and acting before delay teaches the wrong norm.

prompts.label: What performance gap was visible and consequential?
What decision or support process did you own?
How did you clarify, coach, document, and decide?
What measurable change happened for the person, team, and organization?
What would you change about your timing, rejected alternative, or approach?

relatedScenarios: A senior IC in a leadership role blocks delegation.
A manager is culturally beloved but delivery-poor.
A director cannot scale from team execution to organizational leadership.
A high-output leader damages trust through blame, intimidation, or peer bypassing.
A VP must choose between protecting a critical roadmap and removing a harmful leader.
